stories.title: The company that invented its own killer, then hid it in a drawer
stories.hook: Kodak built the first digital camera in 1975. Then buried it for 20 years.
stories.body:
In 1975, a young Kodak engineer named Steven Sasson built a toaster-sized device that could capture an image without film. It took 23 seconds to record a black-and-white photo onto a cassette tape. He carried it into a room of Kodak executives, demonstrated it, and got a memorable response: it was 'cute,' but why would anyone want to look at photos on a television screen when they could hold a print in their hand?

That single reaction shaped the next two decades. Kodak did not fail to see digital photography coming, it invented digital photography. What it lacked was a reason to want it to succeed. Film and processing were roughly two-thirds of Kodak's profit. Every executive in that room understood, correctly, that a good digital camera would shrink that business. So the company did what most companies do when a new technology threatens the thing that pays everyone's salary: it funded digital research quietly, kept it years behind what was technically possible, and spent its real energy defending film.

The rest of the industry did not wait. Canon, Sony, and eventually camera phones moved digital imaging forward without a legacy film business to protect. By the time Kodak tried to pivot seriously in the 2000s, consumers had already rebuilt their habits around formats Kodak did not control. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2012, having invented, patented, and then essentially sat on the technology that ended it.

This is the textbook case behind Clayton Christensen's idea of the innovator's dilemma: it is not that incumbents fail to see disruption coming. It is that their existing customers, existing profit centers, and existing incentive structures actively reward them for ignoring it. Rational short-term decisions, made by smart people, compound into a company that cannot save itself. The lesson is not 'innovate faster.' It's that the thing most likely to kill a market leader is a decision that looks completely sensible on this year's income statement.

The same shape shows up constantly. A newspaper protecting print ad revenue while it slow-walks digital. A taxi commission protecting medallion values while ignoring ride-hailing apps. A cable company slow-rolling streaming to protect bundle pricing. Once you've seen the Kodak pattern, you start noticing it everywhere a profitable business is asked to compete with its own replacement.
stories.sayThis: Kodak didn't miss digital photography, they invented it in 1975 and shelved it, because it would have cannibalized film. That's the real innovator's dilemma: it's not blindness, it's rational incentives protecting the wrong thing.

stories.title: Why the company that basically invented modern AI research let a startup get there first
stories.hook: Google published the research behind ChatGPT. Then held back its own chatbot for years.
stories.body:
The core architecture behind ChatGPT, the transformer, comes from a 2017 paper written by Google researchers, titled 'Attention Is All You Need.' Google was arguably the best-positioned company on earth to ship a conversational AI product. It had the research, the compute, and years of head start. And yet when OpenAI's ChatGPT launched in November 2022 and crossed 100 million users faster than almost any consumer product in history, Google was reportedly caught off guard enough internally that leadership declared a 'code red.'

The technology wasn't the gap. The business model was. Google's core revenue engine is search ads, a model built on showing you a page of links and charging advertisers when you click one. A chatbot that simply answers your question in one confident paragraph, with no links to click, is structurally at odds with that. Every serious internal push toward a more conversational search experience ran into the same question: if this works too well, doesn't it eat the thing that makes us money? Reporting at the time described exactly this tension slowing Google's public rollout of conversational AI, even as it had working versions internally.

OpenAI had no such conflict. It had no search ad business to protect, no billions in quarterly revenue tied to the ten blue links. It could ship something that cannibalized nothing, because it had nothing yet to cannibalize. That asymmetry, not raw technical capability, is what let a much smaller company move first on a technology the giant had largely invented.

Google did respond, eventually, with Gemini and AI-powered search summaries, and has since poured enormous resources into catching up. But the sequence is the more interesting story than the current scoreboard: the incumbent with the deepest research bench in the world still got outrun on its own invention, because moving first would have meant competing with itself.

It's the same structural bind as Kodak and film, just running at software speed instead of over twenty years. The size of the threat to your existing revenue predicts your speed far better than the size of your R&D budget does.
stories.sayThis: Google invented the transformer, the actual architecture behind ChatGPT. What slowed them down wasn't capability, it was that a great conversational answer has no links to click, and their whole business is built on the click.

stories.title: The oldest wrong idea in economics, and why it keeps coming back for every new technology
stories.hook: Every generation is sure this machine will finally run out of jobs for people.
stories.body:
In the early 1800s, English textile workers called Luddites smashed mechanical looms, convinced that machines would permanently take their work and leave nothing behind. The same fear resurfaced almost word for word with the tractor, with the personal computer, with outsourcing, and now with AI. Economists have a name for the assumption underneath all of it: the lump of labor fallacy, the belief that there is a fixed amount of work to be done in an economy, so if a machine (or a country, or an algorithm) does some of it, there is necessarily less left for humans.

The assumption is intuitive and almost always wrong, historically. The amount of 'work available' in an economy is not a pie of fixed size. When a technology makes one kind of labor dramatically cheaper or faster, it doesn't just remove jobs, it also lowers costs, raises productivity, and frees up money and time that gets spent elsewhere, which creates new demand and new categories of work nobody had a name for yet. Bank tellers are the classic modern example: ATMs were supposed to eliminate them starting in the 1970s. Instead, ATMs made it cheaper to run a branch, so banks opened more branches, and total teller employment in the U.S. was, decades later, higher than before ATMs existed, though the job itself shifted from cash-handling to sales and service.

This doesn't mean automation and AI are painless. It absolutely displaces specific people from specific jobs, often fast, often without a clear next step for the individual affected, and that pain is real and worth taking seriously. The fallacy isn't in worrying about disruption, it's specifically in the arithmetic that says 'X tasks automated equals X jobs permanently gone,' as if the rest of the economy just sits still and absorbs the loss instead of reorganizing around the new cost structure.

The honest, more useful question isn't 'will AI take jobs' (some jobs, yes, definitely). It's 'what new demand gets created by the cost and speed AI unlocks, and who is positioned to do that new work.' That's a harder question, and a much better one to be asking in a room full of people confidently doing the fixed-pie math out loud.
stories.sayThis: That's the lump of labor fallacy, the assumption that there's a fixed amount of work to go around. ATMs were supposed to end bank tellers, employment actually went up because branches got cheaper to run and banks opened more of them.

stories.title: The more efficient something gets, the more of it people use, not less
stories.hook: Cheaper compute doesn't shrink demand for compute. It explodes it.
stories.body:
In 1865, a British economist named William Stanley Jevons noticed something that seemed backwards. James Watt's improved steam engine used coal far more efficiently than earlier designs, which should have meant Britain burned less coal. Instead, total coal consumption exploded. A more efficient engine made steam power cheap enough to use in far more places, for far more purposes, than anyone had before, and the total volume of use grew faster than the efficiency gain shrank it. This became known as Jevons paradox: making a resource more efficient to use can increase total consumption of it, not decrease it.

The pattern has repeated with almost comic regularity. More fuel-efficient cars didn't reduce total gasoline use as much as predicted, because cheaper-to-run cars encouraged more driving and bigger vehicles. Faster, cheaper internet didn't reduce data traffic, it created streaming video, which uses vastly more bandwidth than the text and images the efficient internet was originally built for. Each efficiency gain doesn't just do the old job cheaper, it unlocks new uses that weren't economical before.

AI compute is currently living through exactly this. Every time a new technique makes running a large model cheaper, per token, per query, the immediate industry reaction isn't 'great, now we'll spend less on compute.' It's the opposite: cheaper inference makes it viable to put AI into products where it was previously too expensive to bother, so total compute demand keeps climbing even as the per-unit cost falls. This is a big part of why chip demand and data center buildout keep accelerating rather than plateauing as models get more efficient.

The practical use of Jevons paradox in a conversation is as a check on lazy efficiency arguments. 'This new technology will reduce X' is often wrong precisely because the technology is good. Efficiency gains tend to expand a market's boundaries rather than just shrinking its costs within the old boundaries, and it's worth asking, for any efficiency story, whether you're looking at the steam engine or the coal pile.
stories.sayThis: That's Jevons paradox: more efficient steam engines didn't cut Britain's coal use, they made steam power cheap enough to use everywhere, so total coal consumption went up. Same thing happening with AI, cheaper inference is driving more compute demand, not less.

stories.title: Why you love the shelf you built more than the identical one you bought assembled
stories.hook: People pay more for things they had a hand in making, even badly.
stories.body:
In a 2011 study, researchers Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely had participants assemble simple IKEA storage boxes, fold origami, and build sets of Legos, then asked them to bid, in an auction, on their own creations versus identical pre-built ones made by someone else. Consistently, people valued the things they built themselves far more than the identical finished version, even when their own effort had produced a visibly clumsy, imperfect object. Non-builders bidding on the same items, seeing both versions with no attachment to either, showed no such preference. The researchers named it the IKEA effect: labor, even mediocre labor, creates disproportionate love for the result.

The effect isn't really about furniture. It shows up anywhere effort precedes ownership. It's a documented reason recipe box subscriptions like Blue Apron work better than fully-cooked meal delivery for building customer loyalty, you did something, so you value the outcome more, and you're more likely to repeat the behavior. It's part of why onboarding flows that ask a new user to build their own dashboard, set preferences, or invite a teammate tend to produce stickier users than ones that hand over a fully pre-configured product on day one. Effort spent up front converts into a felt sense of ownership that a flawless out-of-the-box experience doesn't generate nearly as well.

There's a boundary condition worth knowing, because it's the part most people leave out when they cite this. The effect requires the task to be completed, not abandoned halfway, and it works better when the effort feels meaningful rather than arbitrarily annoying. Forcing a customer through pointless friction doesn't create the IKEA effect, it just creates frustration; the effort has to feel like it's building something the person actually wanted to build.

The honest takeaway for anyone in product or marketing isn't 'add more setup steps.' It's that a small, well-designed moment of effortful participation, customizing something, naming something, assembling something, tends to be worth more to the relationship than a slicker but entirely passive handoff.
stories.sayThis: That's the IKEA effect, people who assemble something themselves value it more than an identical pre-built version, even when their own build looks worse. It's a big reason products with a little setup effort tend to retain better than ones that hand you a finished experience.

stories.title: Losing $20 hurts roughly twice as much as finding $20 feels good
stories.hook: The same amount of money, framed as a loss instead of a gain, changes behavior completely.
stories.body:
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky ran an experiment where people were offered a coin flip: heads, you lose $100, tails, you win some amount. Most people demanded a potential win of around $200 or more before they'd take the bet, even though it's a mathematically fair coin flip. That asymmetry, roughly a two-to-one weighting of losses over equivalent gains, is the empirical basis for loss aversion, part of the prospect theory work that won Kahneman the Nobel Prize in Economics. The core finding: humans are not neutral calculators of gains and losses, we feel a loss of a given size more intensely than we feel an equivalent gain.

This single asymmetry quietly explains a huge amount of consumer behavior once you know to look for it. A free trial that gives you full access for 14 days and then asks you to pay is exploiting loss aversion far more effectively than a paid trial that unlocks features, because canceling now feels like losing something you already have, rather than declining to buy something new. 'Members save $40' is a weaker frame than 'Non-members pay $40 more,' identical math, different psychological weight. Airline status tiers, streaming bundles, retirement default enrollment, all of them are built, deliberately, around the fact that people work harder to avoid a loss than they will to capture an equivalent gain.

It also explains a lot of bad decision-making that has nothing to do with marketing. Investors hold falling stocks too long, hoping to 'get back to even,' because selling at a loss feels far worse than an unrealized loss sitting on paper, even though the money is functionally already gone either way. Negotiators walk away from good deals because a concession framed as 'giving something up' feels worse than an identical outcome framed as 'both sides gaining.'

The practical version of this concept in a business conversation is simple: how you frame an identical outcome, as an avoided loss versus an achieved gain, changes how people respond to it, often dramatically, even though nothing about the actual numbers has changed.
stories.sayThis: That's loss aversion, Kahneman's research found people weigh a loss about twice as heavily as an equivalent gain. It's why 'don't lose access' framing in a cancellation flow converts so much better than 'unlock more features' framing, even for the exact same offer.

stories.title: Why lipstick sales go up when the economy goes down
stories.hook: In every recession on record, small indulgences sell better, not worse.
stories.body:
Leonard Lauder, chairman of Estee Lauder, is credited with popularizing an observation after the September 11 attacks and the 2001 recession: lipstick sales rose even as overall consumer spending pulled back. He'd noticed the same pattern going back to the Great Depression, when lipstick sales reportedly climbed even as unemployment soared. The pattern held again in the 2008 financial crisis and, in a modern variant, during COVID lockdowns, when 'lipstick' effectively became skincare and at-home beauty products, since nobody was leaving the house to show off lipstick, but plenty of people still wanted a small, affordable act of self-care.

The explanation economists settled on isn't that people get vain during hard times. It's that when consumers can no longer justify big-ticket purchases, a new car, a vacation, a home renovation, they don't stop wanting to feel good about spending money. Instead, spending shifts down-market toward small, affordable luxuries that deliver a disproportionate emotional return relative to their cost. A $28 lipstick is a treat that fits inside a tightened budget in a way a $2,000 handbag no longer does. The desire for a little indulgence doesn't disappear in a downturn, it gets rerationed into the cheapest available form of it.

This reshapes which categories actually get hurt in a recession, and it's frequently counterintuitive. Mid-tier categories, the ones too expensive to feel like a treat but not essential enough to be a necessity, tend to get hit hardest. Meanwhile, both the very cheap indulgence categories (candy, cosmetics, streaming subscriptions) and, oddly, some ultra-luxury categories catering to buyers whose wealth is largely insulated from a downturn, can hold up comparatively well. It's the middle that gets squeezed.

The lipstick effect is a genuinely useful lens any time someone claims a recession will simply crush 'discretionary spending' as one uniform category. It doesn't. It reallocates discretionary spending toward the cheapest available form of feeling okay, and understanding which specific products play that role in a given market is a much sharper read on consumer behavior than a blanket 'people stop spending' story.
stories.sayThis: That's the lipstick effect, first named by Estee Lauder's chairman after 9/11. Recessions don't kill the desire for small indulgences, they push spending down-market toward the cheapest version of feeling good, which is why affordable treats often hold up while mid-tier categories get crushed.

stories.title: The pandemic didn't make people want less stuff, it made them want different stuff
stories.hook: Two years indoors permanently rewired what people are willing to pay a premium for.
stories.body:
During COVID lockdowns, with restaurants, travel, concerts, and gyms shut down, household spending didn't vanish, it redirected almost entirely into physical goods: home fitness equipment, kitchen appliances, home office gear, loungewear. Peloton and other home-fitness brands saw huge demand spikes. Furniture and appliance retailers had some of their strongest years on record. Consumers, unable to spend on experiences, poured money into upgrading the physical space they were now confined to.

The moment restrictions lifted, the pattern didn't just normalize, it overcorrected hard in the other direction. Travel bookings, restaurant reservations, and live event ticket sales surged well past pre-pandemic levels, a phenomenon widely labeled 'revenge spending' or 'revenge travel.' Airlines and hotels posted some of their strongest pricing years ever in 2022 and 2023, even as inflation squeezed budgets elsewhere, because people were actively choosing to prioritize experiences they'd been denied, sometimes cutting other spending to afford it.

What makes this more than a temporary blip is what it reveals about the underlying shift: survey and spending data through the mid-2020s consistently showed a durable move in discretionary budgets away from goods and toward experiences, described by many retail analysts as an acceleration of the 'experience economy' trend that was already building before COVID. Having been forced to live without concerts, travel, and dining out, a meaningful share of consumers came out the other side actively re-ranking experiences above physical goods in their spending priorities, not just catching up on missed time, but genuinely reallocating going forward.

This matters well beyond travel and hospitality. It shows up in how younger consumers describe wanting to spend a bonus (an experience over an object), in the growth of experience-based gifting, and in retail brands increasingly building physical stores around events and activities rather than just shelves of product, because the thing being sold is increasingly the experience of being there, not only the item you leave with.

The broader lesson: a single forced shock, like a lockdown, doesn't just cause a temporary spending swing. It can permanently move where people believe their money is best spent, and those shifted priorities tend to outlast the event that caused them by years.
stories.sayThis: COVID didn't shrink discretionary spending, it redirected it twice, first into home goods during lockdown, then into 'revenge spending' on travel and experiences once things reopened. And the experience-over-goods shift has stuck around well past the reopening bump.

stories.title: The napkin sketch that explains how Amazon out-competed everyone at once
stories.hook: Jeff Bezos allegedly drew this on a napkin. It became the backbone of Amazon's strategy.
stories.body:
The story goes that in Amazon's early years, Jeff Bezos sketched a simple loop of arrows on a napkin during a dinner conversation with an early advisor: lower prices lead to more customer visits, more customer visits attract more third-party sellers wanting access to that traffic, more sellers mean more selection, more selection improves the customer experience, which drives more traffic, which allows Amazon to lower its cost structure further, which allows lower prices again. Each part of the loop feeds the next part, and the whole loop reinforces itself. This became known internally, and eventually publicly, as Amazon's flywheel.

The metaphor is deliberate and precise, not just a diagram of a business model. A physical flywheel, a heavy spinning disc used in old machinery to store energy, is brutally hard to get moving. Every early push feels like it accomplishes almost nothing, because you're fighting inertia. But each additional push adds momentum that doesn't disappear, it compounds, and eventually the wheel is spinning fast enough that it takes relatively little effort to keep it going, and enormous effort for a competitor to spin up a rival wheel from a standing start. Jim Collins, who popularized flywheel thinking in his book Good to Great, described great companies less as the result of one dramatic breakthrough and more as the result of consistently pushing the same wheel in the same direction long enough for compounding to take over.

The reason this framework is genuinely useful, not just a nice story, is that it forces a specific kind of strategic question: which one variable, if you improved it, would strengthen every other part of your loop, rather than just improving in isolation? Amazon's answer was price and selection, driven by scale. A different company's answer might be community, or content, or network density. The flywheel framework only has teeth when a team can name the actual loop; drawing a generic circle of arrows labeled 'growth' and 'more growth' is not a flywheel, it's decoration.

Worth noting for accuracy: whether Bezos literally drew it on a napkin is company lore that's repeated constantly but not independently confirmed, the underlying strategic logic, however, is extremely well documented in Amazon's own shareholder letters and strategy.
stories.sayThis: That's the Amazon flywheel, lower prices drive traffic, traffic attracts more sellers, more sellers mean more selection, better selection drives more traffic, and the lower cost structure funds lower prices again. The framework only means something if you can name your actual loop, not just draw a generic circle of arrows.

stories.title: Nobody buys a milkshake, they hire it for a job
stories.hook: A famous consulting study found the real competitor to McDonald's milkshake wasn't other milkshakes.
stories.body:
A well-known study, often cited by Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen, was commissioned to help McDonald's boost milkshake sales. The traditional approach was to segment milkshake buyers by demographics and ask them what they'd want improved, thicker, more chocolatey, cheaper, and McDonald's tested those changes with little effect on sales. So the researchers tried something different: they tracked when milkshakes were actually purchased and interviewed the buyers about what else was going on in their life at that exact moment.

The finding was strange at first. Nearly half of all milkshakes were bought before 8:30am, by commuters, alone, who didn't buy anything else with it. Interviewed, these buyers described the same underlying need: a long, boring commute, one free hand, and hunger that needed to last until lunch. A banana got eaten too fast and wasn't filling. A bagel required two hands and left crumbs. Candy bars caused a guilt spike and didn't last. The milkshake, thick, slow to drink through a straw, filling, one-handed, quietly beat all of them at the actual job the commuter needed done: something to occupy a long drive and hold off hunger.

Critically, the milkshake's real competitors weren't other milkshakes, or even other breakfast items in the narrow sense. They were bananas, bagels, boredom, and a bad commute. Once McDonald's understood the job the product was actually being hired for, the useful improvements became obvious and completely different from the original 'make it more chocolatey' brief: make it even thicker so it lasts longer through the commute, and move the dispenser to be faster to grab on the way out.

This case became the founding example for what Christensen called Jobs to Be Done theory, the idea that customers don't buy products because of their category or features, they 'hire' a product to make progress on a specific job in a specific context, and that job is frequently invisible if you only ask people what they want improved about the product they're already buying. It's a genuinely different research method than a features survey: instead of asking what people want, you study the moment of purchase and ask what circumstance they were struggling with when they reached for this thing instead of something else.
stories.sayThis: That's the classic Jobs to Be Done case: McDonald's found half their milkshakes were bought before 8:30am by commuters, and the milkshake's real competitor wasn't other milkshakes, it was bananas and bagels, because the actual job was 'something filling and one-handed for a boring commute.'

stories.title: Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by incompetence
stories.hook: A one-line filter that instantly makes you sound calmer and sharper in any workplace conflict.
stories.body:
The line is usually credited to Robert J. Hanlon, who submitted it to a joke book compilation in 1980, though close variants of the sentiment appear earlier, including in Robert Heinlein's writing. Whatever its exact origin, the idea has stuck around because it's a genuinely useful default filter: when something goes wrong, a missed deadline, a rude email, a broken promise, don't reach for the explanation that someone meant to hurt you. Reach first for the much more common explanation, that someone was overwhelmed, misinformed, distracted, or simply bad at their job in that moment.

The reason this matters more than it sounds is that human brains are wired to over-detect intent. It's a known bias, sometimes described as the fundamental attribution error, where we explain other people's failures with their character ('they're careless, they don't respect my time') while explaining our own identical failures with our circumstances ('I was slammed, the brief was unclear'). Hanlon's razor is a deliberate correction against that asymmetry: apply the same generous, circumstantial explanation to others that you'd automatically apply to yourself, before assuming malice.

It's not a claim that malice never exists, obviously it does, and the razor isn't meant to be used to excuse genuinely bad actors indefinitely. It's a starting heuristic, a first filter to run before escalating a disagreement, because assuming malice tends to produce defensive, accusatory responses that make a merely incompetent situation worse, while assuming incompetence tends to produce clarifying, problem-solving responses that actually fix things. If you open a conversation assuming someone was careless rather than assuming they were hostile, you get very different, and usually much more productive, next sentences.

In a business context specifically, it's a genuinely practical tool for reading a missed deliverable, a terse Slack message, or a vendor dropping the ball: run the incompetence explanation first, it's statistically more often correct, and even when it turns out to be wrong, you haven't burned the relationship finding that out.
stories.sayThis: Hanlon's razor: never attribute to malice what's adequately explained by incompetence. It's a good default any time a missed deadline or a curt email makes you want to assume someone's out to get you, the boring explanation is usually the right one.

stories.title: The moment a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure
stories.hook: Every KPI you've ever seen gamed traces back to this one idea.
stories.body:
British economist Charles Goodhart proposed the original version of this idea in 1975 in the context of monetary policy, but it's usually quoted today in the compressed form popularized by anthropologist Marilyn Strathern: 'when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' The logic is simple once stated: a metric works as a proxy for something you actually care about only as long as nobody is optimizing directly for the metric itself. The instant it becomes the target people are managed and paid against, people find the cheapest way to move the number, which is often disconnected from the real outcome the number was supposed to represent.

The example often told, possibly apocryphal but genuinely useful as an illustration, involves Soviet nail factories that were given production quotas measured by weight. Factories responded by producing a small number of enormous, useless nails, technically hitting the quota, while making almost nothing anyone could actually use. Whether or not that specific story is literally true, the mechanism it illustrates is extremely well documented across real organizations: a customer support team measured on average call handling time will get faster average call times, partly by resolving issues efficiently, and partly by transferring difficult calls to someone else's queue or hanging up early. A sales team measured purely on leads generated will generate a lot of low-quality leads. A hospital measured on wait times will sometimes reclassify how it counts a 'wait.'

The fix isn't 'don't measure anything,' that's not realistic or useful advice. It's to treat any single metric with suspicion once people know it's being watched, and to pair metrics that could be gamed against each other, so gaming one makes another one visibly worse. A support team measured on both handling time and customer satisfaction can't quietly transfer calls without satisfaction dropping. A sales team measured on both lead volume and lead-to-close conversion can't pad the top of the funnel without the conversion number exposing it.

Goodhart's law is one of the most useful concepts to know by name in any strategy or operations conversation, because it explains, precisely, why so many well-intentioned KPI systems quietly produce behavior nobody actually wanted.
stories.sayThis: That's Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. It's why single-KPI systems get gamed so reliably, you almost always need a paired metric that makes gaming the first one visible.

stories.title: The $50 million meeting Blockbuster laughed out of the room
stories.hook: Netflix's founders once offered to sell to Blockbuster. Blockbuster said no.
stories.body:
In 2000, Netflix was a small, unprofitable DVD-by-mail startup burning cash. As Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph has recounted, he and Reed Hastings flew to Dallas to pitch Blockbuster CEO John Antioco on a deal: Blockbuster would acquire Netflix for roughly $50 million, and Netflix would effectively become Blockbuster's online arm. By most retellings, Antioco and his team didn't take the offer seriously, Netflix's business, mailing DVDs in red envelopes, looked like a niche curiosity next to Blockbuster's thousands of stores and dominant market position.

Blockbuster wasn't wrong that its own model worked, at the time. In 2000, Blockbuster had roughly 9,000 stores and a market cap in the billions. Late fees alone reportedly generated hundreds of millions of dollars a year in revenue, a number that, in hindsight, should have been a warning sign rather than a comfort: a meaningful chunk of Blockbuster's profit came from a customer pain point, not from a service its customers loved. Netflix's entire early value proposition was implicitly an attack on that exact pain point, no due dates, no late fees.

Blockbuster didn't ignore online video entirely, it eventually launched its own DVD-by-mail and digital efforts years later, but by then Netflix had a multi-year head start in logistics, recommendation data, and brand association with the category. Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010. Netflix, the company it once could have bought for $50 million, was worth well over $10 billion within a few years of that filing, and is worth vastly more today.

The strategic error wasn't failing to predict streaming, almost nobody predicted the specifics of streaming in 2000. It was evaluating an acquisition target purely by its current size relative to your own, rather than by whether it neutralized a real vulnerability in your own model. A dominant incumbent's biggest blind spot is often not a competitor that looks strong today, it's a small one quietly attacking the exact thing propping up the incumbent's profits.
stories.sayThis: Netflix reportedly offered to sell itself to Blockbuster for about $50 million in 2000, and Blockbuster passed. The lesson isn't hindsight bias, it's that Blockbuster evaluated Netflix by its current size instead of by whether it neutralized Blockbuster's biggest actual vulnerability: late fees.

stories.title: The memo a CEO wrote to tell his own company it was dying
stories.hook: Nokia's CEO compared his own company to a man on a burning oil rig, to his own employees.
stories.body:
In February 2011, Nokia CEO Stephen Elop published an internal memo to the entire company that leaked publicly almost immediately, an unusually blunt move for a CEO communicating to his own workforce. Elop opened with an analogy: a man standing on a burning oil platform in the North Sea, who has to make an urgent choice between staying on a platform he knows is failing or jumping into freezing water with uncertain survival odds. The man jumps. Elop's point was direct: Nokia, once the dominant mobile phone maker in the world, was standing on a burning platform of its own, and continuing to do what it had always done was no longer a safe option.

The specifics were stark. Nokia's Symbian operating system, which had powered its smartphones for years, was losing ground fast to Apple's iOS and Google's Android, both of which offered developers and consumers a fundamentally more modern app and interface experience. Nokia had genuine engineering talent and enormous market share in raw phone sales, but its software platform, the layer that increasingly determined whether a phone felt current or obsolete, had fallen behind in a way hardware excellence alone couldn't fix.

The memo announced what came next: Nokia would abandon Symbian and partner with Microsoft, adopting Windows Phone as its primary smartphone platform. The bet did not work. Windows Phone never built a competitive app ecosystem against iOS and Android's already-dominant developer bases, and Nokia's phone business continued to shrink. Microsoft acquired Nokia's devices business in 2013, and by 2016 the Nokia-branded smartphone business as it had existed was effectively gone, folded and later revived under a different licensing arrangement with other manufacturers.

What makes this case genuinely useful beyond the collapse itself is the memo's honesty about the actual mechanism of decline: it wasn't a single competitor's product feature. It was a platform-level dependency, an operating system and developer ecosystem, that had quietly become the real basis of competition while Nokia kept optimizing the layer, hardware, that mattered less each year. Recognizing which layer of the stack competition has moved to, before the numbers make it obvious, is the entire strategic problem the burning platform memo was trying, correctly but too late, to name.
stories.sayThis: Nokia's CEO wrote an internal memo comparing the company to a man on a burning oil platform, forced to jump into freezing water because staying was worse. The real lesson: Nokia kept winning on hardware while competition had already moved to the software/app-ecosystem layer, and by the time that was undeniable, it was close to too late.

stories.title: The company that invented the modern computer interface and let everyone else sell it
stories.hook: Xerox built the mouse, the GUI, and Ethernet in the 1970s. Apple and Microsoft made the money.
stories.body:
Xerox PARC, the research lab Xerox founded in Palo Alto in 1970, produced an extraordinary concentration of foundational computing technology in a single decade: the graphical user interface with overlapping windows and icons, the computer mouse as a practical input device, Ethernet networking, and the laser printer, among others. Researchers at PARC built the Xerox Alto in 1973, a working personal computer with a graphical interface, years before anything resembling it reached consumers.

Xerox's core business was copiers, an extremely profitable one, and the company's leadership and sales structure were built around that business, not around personal computing. When Xerox did eventually try to commercialize PARC's work, the Xerox Star, released in 1981, it was priced at roughly $16,000, positioned for large corporate customers, and sold in small numbers. The technology was real and years ahead of the market; the go-to-market strategy and pricing were not built for the audience that would eventually make graphical computing ubiquitous.

Steve Jobs famously visited Xerox PARC in 1979, as part of an arrangement where Xerox's venture capital arm invested in Apple in exchange for Apple engineers getting a look at PARC's work. Jobs and his team saw the GUI and mouse concepts and moved quickly to adapt them into the Lisa and then the far more successful Macintosh, released in 1984 at a fraction of the Xerox Star's price and aimed squarely at a broader market. Microsoft's Windows followed a similar interface logic later in the decade, extending the graphical paradigm to the much larger IBM-compatible PC market.

The strategic lesson isn't simply "Xerox was slow." It's that invention and commercialization are genuinely different capabilities, requiring different incentive structures, and a company optimized to sell one thing exceptionally well (copiers, at high margins, to enterprise buyers) is often structurally unable to see, price, or distribute a genuinely different kind of product, even one built in its own labs by its own engineers. The value didn't leak to competitors because Xerox lacked talent or vision. It leaked because the organization built to sell copiers had no natural path to sell a $500 computer to a home user, and nothing internally was rewarded for finding one.
stories.sayThis: Xerox PARC invented the GUI, the mouse, and Ethernet in the 1970s, years before Apple or Microsoft. The company built to sell high-margin copiers to enterprises had no organizational path to sell an affordable computer to a home user, invention and commercialization are different muscles, and Xerox only had one of them.

stories.title: The chip company that turned down the iPhone
stories.hook: Intel's CEO later called this one decision the biggest regret of his career.
stories.body:
In a 2013 interview with The Atlantic, former Intel CEO Paul Otellini revealed that Apple had approached Intel to build the processor for the original iPhone before its 2007 launch. Intel declined. Otellini's explanation, as he described it, wasn't a failure of engineering confidence, it was a forecasting decision. Apple's price point for the chip didn't match what Intel's internal models projected the iPhone would sell in volume, and at the volumes Intel was forecasting, the deal didn't clear Intel's profitability bar. Otellini said plainly, in hindsight, that the volume estimates were wrong by an enormous margin, and that turning the deal down was the decision he most regretted.

The iPhone went on to sell in the hundreds of millions of units annually within a few years, and smartphone chips became one of the largest and most strategically important semiconductor markets in the world, a market Intel subsequently spent enormous resources trying, and largely failing, to break into through its own mobile chip efforts. ARM-based chip designs, not Intel's x86 architecture, came to dominate mobile, and Intel's absence from that market is now considered one of the most consequential missed opportunities in the company's history.

What makes this case more useful than a simple "they should have said yes" story is the mechanism of the error. Intel didn't dismiss the iPhone as a bad product or Apple as a weak partner. It ran a standard, rational forecasting process, the kind that had served Intel well for the PC market for decades, and that process produced a volume estimate that was wrong by roughly two orders of magnitude. The tool that made Intel excellent at judging the PC chip market was the same tool that failed catastrophically when pointed at a genuinely new category with no historical base rate to anchor on.

This is a specific and common trap for large, successful companies: the forecasting and evaluation processes built from years of data in an existing market are often the least reliable instrument available for judging an unprecedented new one, precisely because they're calibrated to a world that the new product is trying to leave behind.
stories.sayThis: Intel turned down building the original iPhone's chip because their volume forecasts didn't support the price Apple wanted. Intel's CEO later called it his biggest regret, the same forecasting process that made Intel great at judging the PC market was badly miscalibrated for a category with no historical precedent.

stories.title: The airline that became a strategy-class case study by refusing to serve meals
stories.hook: Every choice Southwest makes reinforces every other choice. That's the whole strategy.
stories.body:
Michael Porter's influential 1996 Harvard Business Review article, 'What Is Strategy?', used Southwest Airlines as its central example of a company competing through a tightly interlocking system of choices rather than any single advantage. Southwest flew short-haul, point-to-point routes between mid-sized cities and secondary airports, skipping the hub-and-spoke model most major airlines relied on. It used only one aircraft type, the Boeing 737, simplifying maintenance, training, and parts inventory. It offered no meals, no seat assignments, and no interline baggage transfers to other airlines.

Each individual choice looks like a cost-cutting measure in isolation. Together, they form a system where each piece reinforces the others: no meals and no seat assignments mean faster boarding and turnaround, faster turnaround means planes spend more time in the air and less time idle at gates, which means Southwest needs fewer aircraft to fly the same number of routes, which lowers capital costs, which subsidizes the low fares that draw the point-to-point, price-sensitive customers the whole system was built around in the first place. Porter's argument was that this fit between activities, not any one activity alone, is what made the strategy difficult to copy.

The proof came from a direct competitive test. Continental Airlines, watching Southwest's success, launched 'Continental Lite' in the early 1990s, adopting some of Southwest's practices: lower fares and no meals on short routes, while keeping its existing hub-and-spoke network, full-service long-haul flights, and travel-agent commission structure running in parallel. The hybrid strategy confused operations, angered travel agents and full-fare customers, and produced chronic delays. Continental Lite was shut down within about two years, a costly failure. Copying isolated pieces of Southwest's model, without rebuilding the entire interlocking system around them, made things worse, not better.

The strategic principle worth carrying into any conversation about competitive advantage: an activity system where the pieces reinforce each other is far more defensible than any single feature or cost advantage, because a competitor can copy one piece cheaply but copying the whole coherent system usually requires rebuilding the company, which is exactly what makes it durable.
stories.sayThis: Southwest's strategy isn't any one thing, no meals, one aircraft type, point-to-point routes, it's that every choice reinforces every other choice. When Continental tried copying just the cheap-fare piece without rebuilding the whole system around it, Continental Lite collapsed within two years. Strategic fit is harder to copy than any single feature.

stories.title: Nintendo stopped competing on graphics and won the console war anyway
stories.hook: While Sony and Microsoft chased processing power, Nintendo chased people who didn't own a console yet.
stories.body:
By the mid-2000s, the video game console market was locked into a well-understood competition: Sony and Microsoft each pushed the PlayStation and Xbox forward primarily on graphical fidelity and processing power, chasing the same core gamer audience with increasingly expensive, increasingly powerful hardware. Nintendo, coming off a console generation where its GameCube had lagged commercially behind both rivals, made a deliberate strategic break from that competition rather than trying to out-power it.

The Wii, released in 2006, was built around motion-sensing controllers instead of raw graphical horsepower, and was deliberately less technically powerful than the PlayStation 3 or Xbox 360 launching around the same time. Nintendo's bet, closely associated with the 'blue ocean strategy' framework developed by W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, was to stop competing for share of the existing gamer market entirely and instead create demand in an adjacent space competitors weren't serving: non-gamers, families, older adults, people who found existing consoles intimidating or irrelevant to them. Wii Sports, bundled with the console, was designed explicitly to be playable by someone who had never held a game controller before.

The strategy worked commercially in a way that surprised much of the industry. The Wii outsold both the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 over the course of the generation, despite being the least technically powerful of the three, because it was drawing from a pool of buyers, first-time console owners and older demographics, that its more powerful competitors were barely reaching. Nintendo didn't win a better version of the existing competition; it changed which competition it was in.

The durable idea, useful well past gaming: when an entire industry converges on competing along the same one or two dimensions, more power, more features, lower price on the same spec sheet, the biggest open opportunity is sometimes not to win that fight better, but to identify a genuinely underserved audience being excluded by the terms of that fight, and build for them instead.
stories.sayThis: While Sony and Microsoft raced each other on raw graphics power, Nintendo built the Wii around motion controls for people who'd never owned a console, and it outsold both. Classic blue ocean strategy: instead of competing harder on the industry's existing terms, they changed which market they were competing in.

stories.title: The company that was about to be broken up, and the outsider who said no
stories.hook: IBM's board was ready to split the company into pieces. Its new CEO refused.
stories.body:
By 1993, IBM was in the worst crisis of its history. The mainframe business that had defined the company for decades was being eroded by cheaper, more distributed computing, personal computers, client-server systems, and IBM posted a loss of roughly $8 billion in 1993, one of the largest corporate losses in U.S. history at the time. Serious internal plans were underway to break IBM into a set of independent 'Baby Blue' companies, each focused on a separate product line, effectively conceding that the integrated IBM of the mainframe era no longer made strategic sense.

Louis Gerstner, hired as CEO in 1993, was notably an outsider to the computer industry, previously running RJR Nabisco and American Express. His first major strategic decision was to reject the breakup plan entirely. Gerstner's read, laid out later in his memoir 'Who Says Elephants Can't Dance,' was that IBM's scattered pieces, kept together, held a distinct and valuable capability that no single product line captured on its own: the ability to design, integrate, and manage complex computing systems end to end for large enterprise customers, hardware, software, and support, as a single relationship, not a shopping list of separate vendors.

That thesis became the foundation for pivoting IBM's center of gravity away from selling hardware boxes and toward selling services and integration, formalized through the growth of IBM Global Services. Instead of competing purely on chip speed or server pricing, IBM increasingly competed on being the single trusted partner that could run a bank's or airline's entire technology backbone, a much harder position for smaller, more specialized competitors to replicate. Within a few years, services became IBM's largest and fastest-growing segment, and IBM avoided the breakup entirely, remaining one of the largest technology companies in the world for decades afterward.

The strategic lesson is specific: turnarounds don't always come from finding a new product. Gerstner's insight was organizational and relational, that the company's real, defensible asset wasn't any individual technology, most of which was becoming commoditized, but the integration and trust relationship no single product-line spinoff could carry on its own.
stories.sayThis: IBM's board was ready to split the company into pieces after an $8 billion loss in 1993. New CEO Lou Gerstner said no, and instead pivoted IBM from selling hardware boxes to selling end-to-end services, because the real defensible asset was the integration relationship with enterprise customers, not any single product.

stories.title: Coca-Cola ran the numbers perfectly and still got it completely wrong
stories.hook: Blind taste tests said the new formula was better. Customers revolted anyway.
stories.body:
In April 1985, Coca-Cola replaced its original formula with a reformulated, sweeter recipe, quickly nicknamed 'New Coke,' after extensive market research. The company had run more than 200,000 blind taste tests, and the new formula consistently beat both the old Coca-Cola recipe and Pepsi in head-to-head taste preference. By the metric Coca-Cola had chosen to optimize, flavor preference in a blind sip test, the decision was well-supported by data.

The public reaction was immediate and overwhelmingly negative. Coca-Cola received tens of thousands of complaint calls and letters, protest groups formed, and media coverage treated the reformulation as a genuine cultural event rather than a minor product tweak. Within roughly ten weeks, Coca-Cola reversed course, reintroducing the original formula as 'Coca-Cola Classic' alongside New Coke, which was quietly phased out over the following years amid continued weak sales.

The gap between the research and the reaction came down to what the taste test actually measured versus what customers were actually buying when they bought a Coke. A blind sip test isolates flavor from everything else, brand history, nostalgia, identity, the ritual of the specific can and taste being 'the real thing.' For many longtime customers, the product they were loyal to was never purely a flavor profile to be optimized in isolation, it was a fixed, dependable piece of their own personal and cultural history, and changing the formula without asking permission felt like being told a memory was wrong.

This is a sharper, more specific case than a generic 'listen to your customers' moral. Coca-Cola did listen to customers, extensively and rigorously, but it asked the wrong question. It asked 'which formula do you prefer in a blind taste test' when the real, unasked question was closer to 'what role does this specific, unchanged product play in your life,' a question no sip test was ever going to surface. Excellent research answering the wrong question can be more dangerous than no research at all, because it produces false confidence.
stories.sayThis: New Coke beat old Coke and Pepsi in over 200,000 blind taste tests, and still triggered a consumer revolt that forced a reversal within ten weeks. The research wasn't wrong, it just answered the wrong question, it measured flavor preference when the real product people were loyal to was the unchanged ritual and identity attached to it.

stories.title: The 244-year-old encyclopedia that got outrun by volunteers working for free
stories.hook: Britannica had the best editors money could buy. It lost to people who weren't paid at all.
stories.body:
Encyclopedia Britannica, first published in 1768, spent much of the twentieth century as the prestige standard in reference publishing, a full print set sold through door-to-door sales for well over a thousand dollars, backed by professional editors and expert contributors, sold partly as a status object for households investing in their children's education. In the early 1990s Britannica was still a highly profitable business built on that premium, expert-curated model.

The first real disruption came from Microsoft, not from a rival encyclopedia publisher. Microsoft Encarta launched in 1993 as a CD-ROM encyclopedia, initially built by licensing a smaller existing encyclopedia and adding multimedia, and it was bundled with Windows PCs or sold cheaply compared to a Britannica print set. Encarta wasn't more authoritative than Britannica, in fact it was considered less comprehensive, but it was dramatically cheaper and more convenient, arriving on a computer households were already buying rather than requiring a separate expensive purchase. Britannica's sales, and specifically its premium positioning, took a serious hit.

The second and larger disruption came from Wikipedia, launched in 2001, built on an entirely different model: free, online, and written and edited collaboratively by volunteers rather than paid experts. Wikipedia's individual articles were, especially in its early years, less reliably authoritative than Britannica's professionally edited entries, and it was criticized heavily on exactly that basis. But it was free, current, searchable, constantly expanding, and available the moment anyone had a question, advantages that mattered more to most day-to-day reference use than marginal gains in editorial authority. Britannica ceased print publication in 2012 after 244 years, moving to an online subscription model serving a far smaller niche than it once dominated.

The strategic pattern here matters beyond publishing: Britannica wasn't beaten by a better version of itself. It was beaten twice, first by a much cheaper, adequate substitute, then by a free, collaboratively produced one, each of which competed on a completely different basis (price and access, then cost and speed) than the dimension, editorial authority, Britannica had spent two centuries optimizing.
stories.sayThis: Britannica dominated for over two centuries on editorial authority, then got disrupted twice, first by Encarta on price, then by Wikipedia on being free and collaborative. Neither disruptor beat Britannica on its own terms, they competed on a completely different dimension Britannica hadn't optimized for.

stories.title: The company that invented shopping from home twice, and still went bankrupt
stories.hook: Sears built the original mail-order empire, and even had an early online store, before losing to both.
stories.term: Failure to Extend a Winning Model
stories.body:
Sears, Roebuck and Company built its original empire on a genuinely disruptive idea: the mail-order catalog, launched in the late 1800s, which let rural Americans, far from city stores, order almost anything from a printed catalog and have it shipped directly to them. It became so central to household life that it was sometimes called the 'Consumer's Bible,' and Sears grew into the largest retailer in the United States for much of the twentieth century, later expanding into physical department stores as car ownership and suburban shopping grew.

What makes Sears's later decline particularly sharp as a case study is that the company did not fail to see the next shifts coming, and in at least one case, tried to lead them. Sears was an early participant in Prodigy, an online service launched through a joint venture with IBM in the mid-1980s that let subscribers browse and purchase from an early digital storefront, years before the commercial internet existed for most consumers. Sears had, in a real sense, already built an early version of e-commerce and mostly let it wither, its core business remained anchored in the physical department store model even as discount retailers and later online retailers built the channels that would eventually displace it.

On one side, Walmart and other discount retailers out-executed Sears on everyday low pricing and supply chain efficiency starting in the 1970s and 80s, taking share of the value-conscious customer Sears had once served well. On the other side, Amazon, decades later, effectively rebuilt Sears's own original insight, buy anything, delivered to your door, without a store visit, on a vastly more efficient digital infrastructure, and captured the customer who wanted convenience and selection. Sears filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2018, having been squeezed from both directions by businesses executing variations on ideas Sears itself had pioneered or previewed.

The strategic lesson is a genuinely uncomfortable one: having invented a category, or even having built an early prototype of what eventually disrupts you, is no protection at all if the core organization stays anchored to the format that made it successful the first time. Recognizing your own original insight when a competitor rebuilds it better is harder than it sounds, because it rarely looks like your old idea by the time it succeeds.
stories.sayThis: Sears invented mail-order shopping from home, and even ran an early online storefront through a joint venture with IBM in the 1980s, then lost to Walmart on price and Amazon on convenience, both of which were essentially better executions of ideas Sears had already tried. Inventing a category doesn't protect you if the core business stays anchored to its old format.

stories.title: The cost of anything is what you gave up to get it
stories.hook: The real price of an MBA isn't tuition. It's two years of salary you didn't earn.
stories.body:
Opportunity cost is one of the oldest ideas in economics and one of the most consistently ignored in everyday decision-making: the true cost of any choice isn't just the money spent on it, it's the value of the next-best alternative you gave up to make that choice. An MBA that costs $150,000 in tuition doesn't actually cost $150,000 to the person taking two years off work to earn it, it costs that plus roughly two years of foregone salary, often the larger number by far.

The reason this matters more than it sounds is that direct costs are visible and foregone alternatives are not, so people systematically underweight them. A company that keeps an underperforming product line alive isn't just spending the direct budget on it, it's spending the attention and engineering time that could have gone toward a stronger opportunity, a cost that never appears on any line item but is frequently larger than the visible one. A founder who keeps grinding on a mediocre idea out of stubbornness is paying an opportunity cost measured in every better idea they didn't pursue during that time.

The practical discipline opportunity cost demands is asking, for any resource already committed, not 'is this worth its direct cost' but 'is this still the best use of this resource compared to what else I could do with it right now.' That second question is harder and gets asked far less often, precisely because the alternative use is invisible while the current use is right in front of you.
stories.sayThis: The real cost of anything isn't what you paid for it, it's the value of the next-best thing you gave up to get it. An MBA doesn't just cost tuition, it costs two years of foregone salary too, that's opportunity cost, and it's usually the bigger, less visible number.

stories.title: Why LeBron James should still pay someone else to mow his lawn
stories.hook: Even if you're better at everything than everyone else, specializing still wins.
stories.body:
David Ricardo laid out the theory of comparative advantage in 1817, and economics professors have been illustrating it with a version of the same thought experiment ever since: imagine LeBron James is not only a better basketball player than his neighborhood lawn care service, but, being a world-class athlete, is also physically capable of mowing his own lawn faster than they could. Does that mean he should mow his own lawn? No, and the reason is the entire point of the theory.

Even though LeBron might have an absolute advantage at lawn mowing, being faster at it than the lawn service, he has a vastly larger comparative advantage at being an elite basketball player and pitchman, activities where an hour of his time is worth far more than an hour of lawn mowing. The lawn service, meanwhile, has a comparative advantage at lawn care relative to their own alternative uses of time, they're not giving up a lucrative endorsement deal to mow a lawn. Both parties are better off if LeBron sticks to basketball and pays someone else to mow, even though he could technically do the second job better himself.

This is the same logic that explains why international trade benefits both a country that is more productive at literally everything and one that isn't: what matters isn't who's absolutely better at a given task, it's each party's relative cost of doing one thing versus their other options. In business terms, it's the core argument for specialization and outsourcing: a company shouldn't necessarily do a task in-house just because it could technically do it well, the real question is whether that time is better spent on the thing where the company's advantage, relative to its own alternatives, is largest.
stories.sayThis: That's comparative advantage: even if you're better than everyone else at literally everything, including tasks outside your specialty, you're still better off specializing in whatever you're relatively best at and paying someone else for the rest. It's why LeBron James shouldn't mow his own lawn even if he'd do it faster than the lawn service.

stories.title: The plane everyone knew would lose money, and kept funding anyway
stories.hook: Britain and France kept pouring money into the Concorde long after the math stopped working.
stories.body:
The Concorde supersonic jet, developed jointly by the British and French governments starting in the 1960s, became so strongly associated with irrational persistence that economists now often call the sunk cost fallacy the 'Concorde fallacy.' Well before the plane entered commercial service in 1976, internal cost projections had already made clear that the program would never be commercially profitable, fuel costs, a limited number of viable routes, and a niche customer base for supersonic travel meant the economics simply didn't work. Both governments kept funding it anyway.

The sunk cost fallacy describes exactly this pattern: continuing to invest in a decision because of the resources already committed to it, money, time, effort, rather than evaluating the decision fresh based only on future costs and benefits from this point forward. Rationally, money already spent is gone regardless of what happens next, it should have zero bearing on whether continuing is a good idea. Psychologically, it feels different, walking away from a project after enormous investment feels like admitting that investment was wasted, so people and institutions keep funding it to avoid that feeling, which usually just adds more waste on top of the original amount.

The Concorde did eventually fly commercially for nearly three decades, but it never came close to recovering its development costs and both governments' national airlines operated it at a loss for much of its life, subsidized in part for national prestige reasons rather than economics. The broader business lesson shows up constantly at a much smaller scale: a failing project greenlit eighteen months and several million dollars ago gets another quarter of funding specifically because of how much has already gone into it, when the only question that should matter is whether the next dollar spent, evaluated completely fresh, is the best use of that dollar right now.
stories.sayThis: That's the sunk cost fallacy, sometimes called the Concorde fallacy after the supersonic jet governments kept funding for decades despite knowing it would never be profitable. Money already spent is gone either way, the only rational question is whether the next dollar is worth spending, and people consistently answer that wrong because walking away feels like admitting the past spending was wasted.

stories.title: Why the first slice of pizza is always better than the tenth
stories.hook: Every additional unit of something is worth less to you than the one before it.
stories.body:
Diminishing marginal utility is one of the foundational ideas in economics, and one of the most intuitive once it's named: the first unit of something you consume typically delivers far more satisfaction than each additional unit after it. The first slice of pizza when you're hungry is genuinely great. The fourth is fine. The eighth, if you somehow get there, might make you feel worse than not eating it at all. The pizza hasn't changed, your marginal benefit from each additional slice has fallen sharply.

The concept, formalized in the 19th century as part of what's sometimes called Gossen's first law, explains a huge range of everyday economic behavior that would otherwise look strange. It's why demand curves slope downward, people are willing to pay more for the first unit of something scarce than for the tenth, so sellers have to lower prices to move additional units. It's why a raise from $40,000 to $50,000 a year tends to feel life-changing while a raise from $400,000 to $410,000, an identical ten thousand dollars, barely registers, the marginal utility of money itself diminishes as you have more of it.

In a business or product context, this idea shows up whenever a company assumes 'more of the good thing' is automatically valued the same by customers throughout. A software product that keeps adding features on top of an already-comprehensive tool is often delivering steeply diminishing value with each addition, even though the development cost per feature stays roughly constant. Recognizing where you are on that curve, whether you're still in the steep, high-value early units or deep into the flat, low-value tail, is a genuinely useful lens for deciding where additional investment is actually worth making.
stories.sayThis: That's diminishing marginal utility, each additional unit of something is worth less to you than the one before it, which is exactly why the first slice of pizza beats the eighth. It's also why a $10,000 raise feels huge at a $40,000 salary and barely noticeable at $400,000, the money's the same, the marginal value isn't.

stories.title: Why a live string quartet costs more today than it did in 1826, even adjusted for inflation
stories.hook: Some jobs simply can't get more productive, and that's exactly why they get expensive.
stories.body:
In the 1960s, economists William Baumol and William Bowen studied the economics of live performing arts and noticed something odd: a string quartet performing a Beethoven piece requires exactly the same four musicians and exactly the same amount of time today as it did two centuries ago. There is no meaningful way to make that performance more 'productive,' you can't have the quartet play the piece in half the time with two musicians instead of four. Manufacturing, meanwhile, has seen enormous productivity gains over the same period, machines and automation let one worker produce vastly more than a worker could two hundred years ago.

The problem this creates, now called Baumol's cost disease, is that wages across an economy tend to rise together, roughly tracking overall productivity growth, because workers in low-productivity-growth sectors like live music, education, and healthcare still need to be paid competitively enough to keep them from leaving for higher-paying, higher-productivity industries. So the string quartet's musicians' wages rise over time even though their actual output per hour hasn't changed at all, which means the cost of live music rises faster than inflation generally, not because of inefficiency or greed, but because of a structural mismatch between wage growth (economy-wide) and productivity growth (sector-specific).

This is one of the most useful, least understood explanations for why certain categories, healthcare, higher education, live entertainment, childcare, keep getting relatively more expensive year after year even as manufactured goods (electronics, clothing, furniture) get relatively cheaper. It's not simply 'these industries are broken.' Many of them are structurally resistant to the kind of productivity gains that hold costs down elsewhere, and cost disease is the mechanism connecting that resistance to their rising price tags. It's a sharper, more accurate explanation than 'inflation' or 'inefficiency' for a huge share of what people experience as certain services becoming unaffordable over time.
stories.sayThis: That's Baumol's cost disease, a string quartet needs the same four musicians for the same amount of time today as in 1826, there's no productivity gain to be had. But wages rise economy-wide with productivity elsewhere, so the quartet's costs rise too, which is a big, underappreciated reason healthcare, education, and live entertainment keep getting relatively more expensive.

stories.title: Why 'too big to fail' made the 2008 crisis worse before it happened
stories.hook: When someone else bears the downside of your risk, you take more of it.
stories.body:
Moral hazard describes a specific, well-documented distortion: when a party is insulated from the full consequences of a risk, they tend to take on more of that risk than they would if they bore the full downside themselves. The concept originated in insurance economics, someone with comprehensive car insurance may drive slightly less cautiously than someone paying every repair bill out of pocket, but its most consequential modern application is the 2008 financial crisis.

In the years leading up to 2008, large financial institutions increasingly bet on complex mortgage-backed securities and took on leverage that, in a worse-case scenario, could threaten the broader financial system. Part of what enabled this risk-taking, economists and regulators later argued, was a widespread implicit belief, inside and outside these institutions, that the largest banks were 'too big to fail,' that the government would step in to prevent their collapse rather than risk a systemic financial meltdown. That belief turned out to be largely correct: the U.S. government did intervene with major bailouts in 2008 to stabilize the financial system. But the expectation of that safety net, held before the crisis, is exactly the mechanism moral hazard describes, an institution insulated from the full downside of a risky bet is structurally incentivized to take bigger bets than one that would bear the full consequences of failure.

The pattern generalizes well beyond banking. Any system where an actor can capture the upside of a risky decision while shifting the downside onto someone else, taxpayers, an employer, a business partner, an insurance pool, creates an incentive to take more risk than is socially or organizationally optimal. Recognizing moral hazard in a deal, a compensation structure, or a policy is essentially asking one question: who bears the downside if this goes badly, and does that match who's making the decision to take the risk in the first place.
stories.sayThis: That's moral hazard, when someone is insulated from the downside of a risk, they take more of it. It's a big part of why large financial institutions kept taking on outsized risk before 2008, the implicit belief that they were 'too big to fail' meant they weren't fully exposed to the consequences of losing that bet.

stories.title: The used car problem that won an economist a Nobel Prize
stories.hook: When sellers know more than buyers, the good stuff can disappear from the market entirely.
stories.body:
In 1970, economist George Akerlof published a paper titled 'The Market for Lemons: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism,' using the used car market to describe a problem that seems small but has enormous implications: what happens to a market when sellers know significantly more about the quality of what they're selling than buyers do. In used cars, 'lemons' is American slang for a car with hidden problems, and the seller almost always knows whether their car is a lemon while the buyer generally can't tell just by looking.

Akerlof's insight was that this information gap doesn't just create a risk of occasionally buying a bad car, it can degrade the entire market. Since buyers can't distinguish good cars from lemons, they're only willing to pay an average price reflecting the mixed quality of what's actually on the market. But that average price is unfairly low for someone selling a genuinely good car, so owners of good cars are more likely to exit the market rather than sell at a discount they don't deserve, leaving a higher proportion of lemons behind, which pushes the average price down further, pushing out more good sellers, in a downward spiral. In the extreme case, the market can shrink dramatically or even collapse, not because good cars don't exist, but because the information asymmetry makes it structurally hard to sell them at a fair price. Akerlof shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Economics largely for this work.

This idea, now called adverse selection, generalizes far beyond cars. It's a foundational reason health insurance markets can struggle when sicker people are more likely to seek coverage than healthy people, insurers know less about individual health than the applicant does, so they can't price accurately, which can push premiums up and heathier people out. It's also a genuinely useful lens on any transaction, hiring, freelance marketplaces, B2B sales, where one side has private information the other side can't verify, and understanding it is often the first step toward designing signals (warranties, certifications, reputation scores) that fix the imbalance.
stories.sayThis: That's the market for lemons, or adverse selection, when sellers know more about quality than buyers do, buyers can only pay an average price, which pushes owners of genuinely good stuff out of the market and leaves more lemons behind, sometimes collapsing the market entirely. George Akerlof won a Nobel Prize for working this out using nothing but the used car market.

stories.title: The broken window that looks like it's good for the economy, and isn't
stories.hook: Destruction creates visible jobs. It also destroys the invisible ones nobody notices are missing.
stories.body:
In 1850, the French economist Frédéric Bastiat published an essay describing a simple scene: a boy breaks a shopkeeper's window. Onlookers console the shopkeeper by pointing out the silver lining, now the glazier will get paid to fix it, and that money will circulate through the economy, benefiting everyone. Isn't breaking windows good for economic activity? Bastiat's point was that this reasoning, obvious and appealing as it sounds, is a fallacy, and naming exactly why has become one of the most useful thinking tools in economics.

The error, Bastiat argued, is only counting what is seen, the glazier's new income, while ignoring what is unseen: the shopkeeper now has to spend money repairing a window instead of on whatever he would otherwise have bought, a new suit, inventory for his shop, anything else. That spending, and the income it would have generated for a tailor or a supplier, simply doesn't happen, it's invisible precisely because it never occurred, so nobody misses it or points to it as a loss. Society ends up with a shopkeeper who has a window (which he already had before it broke) instead of a window and a new suit. Total wealth is lower, not higher, even though visible economic activity, the glazier's job, appears to have increased.

The broken window fallacy is invoked constantly, and often wrongly, in debates about whether disasters, wars, or destruction are secretly good for an economy because of the rebuilding activity they generate. The rebuilding is real and visible. What's missing from that accounting is everything that would have been built or bought instead, if the destruction hadn't forced that spending to happen. It's a genuinely sharp tool for catching a very common, very intuitive economic mistake: mistaking redirected spending, forced by a loss, for newly created wealth.
stories.sayThis: That's the broken window fallacy, Bastiat's 1850 point that a broken window creates visible work for a glazier, but the shopkeeper's now spending money on repairs instead of something else, spending that's invisible precisely because it never happens. It's why 'disasters boost the economy' arguments almost always miss the bigger, unseen cost.

stories.title: The question that won a Nobel Prize: why do companies exist at all?
stories.hook: If markets are so efficient, why doesn't everyone just freelance for everything?
stories.body:
