The project's team, including the test's lead officer, referenced the sentiment in a subsequent press conference discussing the project's safety record, and the phrase spread and generalized from there into the broader, more fatalistic form familiar today.

While popularly treated as a humorous fatalistic observation about the universe's tendency toward misfortune, Murphy's Law has a genuinely useful, more serious engineering interpretation underneath the joke: in any sufficiently complex system with enough possible failure points, if a particular failure mode is physically possible, it will eventually occur given enough time, attempts, or scale, a principle taken seriously in fields like aerospace and safety engineering, where design processes explicitly work to identify and eliminate every possible incorrect configuration, rather than relying on operators to simply avoid mistakes through care alone.

The practical, non-fatalistic business application is closely related to defensive design generally: rather than treating a rare edge case or unlikely error as safe to ignore because it's improbable in any single instance, systems and processes handling enough volume or repetition will eventually encounter even a low-probability failure mode, which is why robust engineering and operational design tends to assume that anything physically possible to go wrong eventually will, and builds explicit safeguards accordingly rather than relying on the low individual probability of any specific failure as sufficient protection.
stories.sayThis: Murphy's Law traces to a real 1949 incident, an engineer named Edward Murphy blaming a technician after sensors got wired backward on a rocket sled test. The serious engineering version underneath the joke is that in any complex system with enough possible failure points, anything physically possible to go wrong eventually will, given enough attempts, which is why rigorous safety engineering assumes that rather than relying on any single failure's low probability as protection.

stories.title: 90% of everything is mediocre, and that's not actually a criticism of any one thing
stories.hook: A science fiction writer's defense of his own genre became a much broader, useful law.
stories.body:
Science fiction author Theodore Sturgeon articulated what's now called Sturgeon's Law around 1957 and 1958, responding to critics who dismissed science fiction as a genre by pointing to the large volume of poor-quality work published within it. Sturgeon's response, commonly paraphrased as 'ninety percent of everything is crud,' or in less polite phrasings, 'crap,' argued that the critics weren't wrong about the volume of mediocre science fiction, but were wrong to treat that as a specific indictment of science fiction as a genre, because the same roughly 90% ratio of mediocre-to-excellent work holds true in essentially every other creative and professional field too, once you actually look honestly at the full output rather than just the small subset of acknowledged classics that get remembered and discussed.

The underlying observation generalizes usefully well beyond its original creative-writing context: any sufficiently large body of output in a given category, restaurants in a city, startups in an industry, research papers in a field, tends to be dominated by mediocre examples, with only a small fraction rising to genuine excellence, not because a specific category is uniquely bad, but simply because that ratio appears to be a fairly consistent, recurring feature of large-scale human output generally.

The practical, useful application of Sturgeon's Law is as a corrective against a specific kind of unfair comparison: judging an entire category, industry, or field by its worst or most mediocre examples, while implicitly comparing a different, more selectively curated category against only its best examples, produces a systematically unfair comparison. A genuinely useful evaluation compares like to like, either the full distribution of output in both categories, or, more usefully in most practical decisions, focuses specifically on identifying the top decile within a given category rather than dismissing the category wholesale based on the unremarkable bulk of it.
stories.sayThis: That's Sturgeon's Law, roughly 90% of everything is mediocre, science fiction writer Theodore Sturgeon's response to critics dismissing his genre for the same reason you could dismiss almost any large body of output if you only looked at the bulk of it rather than the top tier. It's a useful check against unfairly comparing one category's average output against another category's curated best examples.

stories.title: Without a clear signal, you genuinely cannot tell parody from sincere extremism online
stories.hook: A well-made joke and a genuine extreme belief can look, and read, identically.
stories.body:
In 2005, a forum poster using the name Nathan Poe made an observation, on a Christian internet discussion board, in the context of debates about creationism and evolution, that has since generalized into a widely cited piece of internet culture: without some explicit, unambiguous signal of the author's actual intent, a satirical exaggeration of an extreme position and a genuine, sincerely held extreme position are frequently indistinguishable from each other in text, particularly online, where tone of voice, facial expression, and other in-person context cues that would normally help signal sarcasm or exaggeration are entirely absent.

The phenomenon, formalized as Poe's Law, captures a genuine, recurring problem in online communication: a well-crafted parody of an extreme political, religious, or ideological position can be so convincingly written that readers mistake it for a sincere expression of that view, and conversely, genuinely sincere extreme statements are frequently mistaken for parody or exaggeration by readers who assume no one could actually, seriously hold that specific view, an assumption that turns out to be unreliable given how genuinely varied real human beliefs actually are.

The practical relevance extends well beyond internet forums into broader questions of online content moderation, misinformation, and media literacy: platforms attempting to distinguish satire from genuine harmful content at scale face a version of exactly this problem, and Poe's Law is frequently invoked as a caution against assuming written text alone, without clearer signals of authorial intent, reliably conveys whether a given statement is meant sincerely or ironically, a limitation with real consequences for how seriously any single piece of online content should be taken at face value without additional context about its source and intent.
stories.sayThis: That's Poe's Law, without a clear signal of intent, a well-crafted parody of an extreme view and a genuinely sincere extreme view are frequently indistinguishable in text, especially online where tone and context cues that would normally signal sarcasm are missing. It's a real, practical problem for content moderation and media literacy generally, text alone often doesn't reliably tell you whether something's meant sincerely or ironically.

stories.title: The fastest way to get the right answer online isn't asking, it's being wrong
stories.hook: People are more motivated to correct a mistake than to answer a question from scratch.
stories.body:
Informally attributed to Ward Cunningham, the inventor of the wiki concept, though Cunningham himself has stated in interviews that he did not actually coin the specific phrasing, crediting it instead to Steven McGeady, the maxim holds that 'the best way to get the right answer on the internet is not to ask a question, it's to post the wrong answer.' The observation, whoever precisely coined it, captures a genuine, widely recognized pattern in online discussion and forum behavior: a neutral, open-ended question frequently goes unanswered or receives only a slow trickle of responses, while a confidently stated but incorrect claim reliably attracts fast, detailed corrections from people motivated specifically to fix the error.

The underlying psychological mechanism is generally understood as an asymmetry in motivation: answering an open question from scratch requires generating an answer with no clear reference point and no obvious payoff beyond general helpfulness, while correcting a visibly wrong statement offers a much more specific, immediate, and satisfying trigger, the discomfort of seeing an error stated confidently and left uncorrected is often a stronger motivator to act than the more diffuse goodwill required to answer a neutral question unprompted.

The practical, if slightly mischievous, application shows up in community management, research, and even internal company knowledge-sharing: rather than posting an open question to a team or community and hoping for engagement, deliberately posting a specific, plausible-but-wrong answer or hypothesis frequently generates faster, more detailed, and more engaged responses than the neutral question would have, precisely because it activates the stronger correction-motivated response rather than relying on the weaker motivation behind answering an open-ended prompt. It's a genuinely useful, evidence-based technique for anyone trying to extract genuine expertise from a group that's otherwise reluctant to proactively volunteer detailed answers.
stories.sayThis: That's Cunningham's Law, the best way to get the right answer online isn't to ask a question, it's to post the wrong answer, since people are far more motivated to correct a confidently stated error than to answer an open question from scratch. It's a genuinely useful, if slightly mischievous, technique for extracting real expertise from a group that's otherwise reluctant to proactively volunteer detailed answers.

stories.title: Software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster
stories.hook: Your new phone is dramatically more powerful than one from a decade ago. It doesn't necessarily feel faster.
stories.body:
Swiss computer scientist Niklaus Wirth discussed the phenomenon that came to bear his name in a 1995 essay titled 'A Plea for Lean Software,' articulating an informal but persistently observed pattern: software tends to become slower, more resource-hungry, and more bloated at a rate that outpaces the rate at which underlying hardware becomes faster and more capable, meaning the actual, felt performance experienced by an everyday user often fails to improve meaningfully over time, and can sometimes even feel worse, despite genuinely enormous, continuous advances in raw hardware capability across the same period.

The mechanism behind the pattern is generally attributed to how software complexity and feature scope tend to expand to consume whatever additional hardware capacity becomes available, a phenomenon with a clear conceptual relative in Parkinson's Law, work expanding to fill available time, applied here to computational resources instead: as processors get faster and memory gets cheaper and more abundant, software developers face less immediate pressure to write efficient, lean code, and features, abstractions, and dependencies accumulate accordingly, consuming the additional hardware headroom that would otherwise have translated into a faster, more responsive felt user experience.

The pattern is a genuinely useful, if slightly uncomfortable, check on a common assumption in technology, that continuous hardware improvement automatically translates into a continuously improving user experience. In practice, the relationship is far more contingent on software engineering discipline than raw hardware specifications alone would suggest, an organization that treats abundant hardware capacity as license to skip efficiency discipline in its own software will frequently deliver a product that feels no faster, or even slower, than an equivalent product built years earlier on meaningfully weaker hardware but with genuinely disciplined, lean engineering practices behind it.
stories.sayThis: That's Wirth's Law, software tends to get slower faster than hardware gets faster, which is why felt performance doesn't automatically improve just because the underlying hardware keeps advancing. It's basically Parkinson's Law applied to computational resources instead of time, software complexity expands to consume whatever extra hardware capacity becomes available, which is why engineering discipline matters more to the actual user experience than raw specs alone.

stories.title: Being told someone will succeed can quietly make it more likely they will
stories.hook: Teachers were given false information about which students would excel. The false information came true anyway.
stories.body:
In a 1968 study, psychologists Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson told elementary school teachers that a randomly selected group of their students had been identified, through a legitimate-sounding but actually fictitious test, as likely to show significant intellectual growth over the coming school year. The selected students were, in reality, chosen entirely at random, with no genuine underlying difference in ability or potential from their classmates. By the end of the year, the randomly labeled 'high potential' students showed measurably greater academic improvement than their peers, purely as a consequence of having been arbitrarily labeled that way at the study's outset.

The explanation researchers offered centered on subtle, largely unconscious behavioral changes in the teachers themselves: teachers holding the belief that a specific student had high potential tended, without necessarily realizing it, to give that student more attention, more encouragement, more challenging material, and more patience during moments of struggle, small behavioral differences that compounded over a full school year into genuinely measurable differences in actual academic outcomes, demonstrating that other people's expectations of a person can causally shape that person's actual real-world performance, not merely their perception of that performance after the fact.

The effect has direct, well-recognized relevance to management and leadership: a manager who genuinely believes a specific employee has high potential tends, often without deliberate intention, to provide more development opportunities, more challenging assignments, and more patient coaching through early mistakes, differential treatment that can become a genuinely self-fulfilling prophecy over time. The uncomfortable flip side, sometimes called the Golem effect, works identically in reverse, an employee a manager has quietly written off as limited tends to receive correspondingly less investment and opportunity, potentially producing exactly the underperformance the manager originally, and possibly incorrectly, expected.
stories.sayThis: That's the Pygmalion effect, Rosenthal and Jacobson randomly told teachers certain students had high potential, no actual difference from their peers, and those randomly labeled students showed measurably greater academic growth by year's end, because the teachers' belief shaped how much attention and patience they unconsciously gave. It works identically in reverse in management too, an employee quietly written off as limited tends to get less investment, which can produce exactly the underperformance that was originally, and possibly wrongly, expected.

stories.title: The longer an online argument runs, the more likely someone brings up Hitler
stories.hook: A law about internet arguments that was formulated back in 1990, before most people had ever been in one.
stories.body:
Attorney and author Mike Godwin formulated Godwin's Law in 1990, stating that as an online discussion or argument grows longer, the probability that someone will make a comparison involving Hitler or Nazis approaches near-certainty. Godwin has explained in later interviews and writing that his original intent was specifically corrective, he wanted to push back against what he saw as the casual, hyperbolic overuse of Nazi comparisons in online arguments over relatively minor or unrelated disagreements, by naming the pattern explicitly and making it a recognizable, somewhat embarrassing thing to be called out for doing.

The law has since become one of the more widely recognized pieces of internet culture and etiquette, frequently invoked in online discussions specifically as a social signal that a particular argument has run long enough, or grown heated enough, to have devolved into exaggerated rhetoric rather than substantive discussion, and in some online communities, informally treated as an implicit concession, being the first party to make a Nazi comparison in an unrelated argument is sometimes treated as effectively losing the discussion by default, a norm that emerged organically from repeated observation of the pattern rather than being formally established by Godwin himself.

The broader, more generalizable lesson underneath the specific, internet-culture-specific example is about rhetorical escalation more generally: as disagreements intensify, particularly in text-based, low-context environments like online forums where genuine nuance and tone are easily lost, participants tend to reach for increasingly extreme comparisons and language to make their point land with more force, a pattern Godwin's Law names specifically for its most common historical form but that generalizes to extreme-comparison escalation in heated arguments generally, worth recognizing as a signal that a discussion has shifted from substance toward pure rhetorical intensity.
stories.sayThis: That's Godwin's Law, formulated in 1990, as an online argument runs longer, the odds someone makes a Nazi or Hitler comparison approach near-certainty. Mike Godwin's actual intent was corrective, naming the pattern to push back against casual overuse of that comparison, and in a lot of online communities it's informally treated as conceding the argument by default. The broader lesson is really about rhetorical escalation generally, extreme comparisons showing up is a signal a discussion has shifted from substance to pure intensity.

stories.title: There's a cognitive limit to how many real relationships a person can maintain
stories.hook: Roughly 150. Past that, an organization needs formal structure, not just trust.
stories.body:
Anthropologist Robin Dunbar's research in the early 1990s proposed a specific cognitive limit on human social relationships, based on observed correlations across primate species between neocortex size, the brain region associated with complex social cognition, and typical social group size within each species. Extrapolating that relationship to humans, Dunbar's research suggested a limit of roughly 150 stable social relationships a person can realistically maintain at once, relationships involving genuine mutual understanding and some ongoing social investment, distinct from the much larger number of names and faces a person might simply recognize without a real relationship attached.

The specific number has drawn both wide popular adoption and legitimate academic scrutiny in the decades since, some subsequent research has questioned the precision and universal applicability of the exact figure, and the underlying primate-brain-size correlation methodology has faced methodological critique, so the number itself is best treated as an approximate, illustrative order of magnitude rather than an exact, universally validated constant.

Despite that legitimate scientific uncertainty around the precise figure, the number is widely cited in business and organizational design contexts specifically because the underlying intuition, informal, trust-based coordination that works well in a small group tends to break down and require more formal management structure once an organization grows past some threshold in that general range, resonates with genuine, widely observed patterns in how companies scale. Many organizations report a felt cultural shift, informal hallway coordination and implicit shared understanding no longer sufficing, roughly somewhere in the low hundreds of employees, a pattern often discussed with reference to Dunbar's number even though the precise figure's scientific standing remains genuinely debated among researchers.
stories.sayThis: That's Dunbar's number, Robin Dunbar's research suggesting a cognitive limit of roughly 150 stable social relationships a person can maintain, based on primate brain size research, though the exact figure has drawn legitimate scientific debate since. It gets cited constantly in organizational design because it resonates with a real, widely observed pattern, informal, trust-based coordination that works fine in a small company tends to break down and need real management structure somewhere in that general range.

stories.title: The longer an idea has already survived, the longer it's likely to keep surviving
stories.hook: For things that don't naturally expire, age itself is evidence of durability, not a reason to expect decline.
stories.body:
The Lindy effect describes a specific, somewhat counterintuitive pattern that applies to non-perishable things, ideas, technologies, institutions, works of art, that don't have a natural, biological expiration point the way a living organism does: for these categories, the longer something has already existed and remained relevant, the longer its expected remaining lifespan tends to be, roughly the opposite intuition from how aging works for a person or a perishable product, where more elapsed time generally predicts less remaining time, not more.

The term is often traced informally to conversations among comedians in New York, reportedly at a delicatessen called Lindy's, about the observed pattern that a comedian's television show or act that had already run for a long time tended to have better odds of continuing than a newer show of the same current popularity, an informal observation about durability rather than a formal academic finding at its origin. The concept was substantially popularized in modern usage through writer and former options trader Nassim Nicholas Taleb, notably in his 2012 book Antifragile, where he applied the idea more broadly to ideas, technologies, and cultural artifacts.

The practical, useful application of Lindy thinking is as a rough heuristic for judging the likely durability of a non-perishable thing under consideration: a business book, technology, or institutional practice that has remained genuinely relevant and actively used for a century is, by Lindy reasoning, a meaningfully better bet to remain relevant going forward than something that's been popular and widely discussed for only the past two years, precisely because survival itself, for non-perishable categories, functions as accumulating evidence of underlying durability rather than as a countdown toward expected decline, the opposite of how most people's intuition, trained mainly on biological and perishable examples, tends to reason about age and remaining lifespan.
stories.sayThis: That's the Lindy effect, for things that don't naturally expire, ideas, technologies, institutions, the longer something has already survived, the longer it's likely to keep surviving, the opposite of how aging works for a living thing. It's a useful heuristic any time you're judging the durability of an idea or practice, something that's stayed genuinely relevant for a century is a better bet going forward than something that's only been popular for the last two years.

stories.title: We always overestimate new technology in the short run, and underestimate it in the long run
stories.hook: The hype cycle and the eventual reality aren't contradictions. They're both true, just on different timelines.
stories.body:
Roy Amara, a researcher and long-serving president of the Institute for the Future, is credited with an observation now widely cited across technology and business forecasting: 'we tend to overestimate the effect of a technology in the short run and underestimate the effect in the long run.' The statement captures a specific, recurring two-part pattern in how new technologies actually play out relative to how they're initially perceived, rather than a simple claim that hype is wrong, it argues hype is wrong about timing in two opposite directions simultaneously, depending on the time horizon being considered.

In the short run, new technologies typically generate intense, often unrealistic expectations, early enthusiasts and media coverage tend to extrapolate rapid, near-term transformation that the technology, still immature, expensive, or poorly integrated into existing systems and behaviors, isn't actually positioned to deliver yet, producing an inevitable period of disillusionment once the gap between hyped expectation and slower actual progress becomes apparent, a pattern closely related to what's sometimes separately described as the technology hype cycle. But Amara's Law's second half is just as important and less commonly emphasized: over a genuinely long time horizon, once the technology matures, gets integrated into complementary systems, and diffuses broadly, its actual cumulative impact frequently exceeds even the most optimistic short-term hype, just realized on a much longer timeline than the initial enthusiasm assumed.

The internet itself is commonly cited as an illustration, 1990s predictions about its near-term transformative impact were, in many specific respects, overstated relative to what actually happened within just a few years, while its actual, multi-decade cumulative transformation of commerce, communication, and daily life ultimately exceeded even those earlier optimistic predictions, just unfolding over twenty-plus years rather than the five the early hype implied. The practical discipline Amara's Law suggests is treating both extremes with appropriate skepticism, dismissing a genuinely important new technology because near-term hype proved overblown, and assuming a slower-than-hyped early rollout means the technology's long-term significance was similarly overstated, are both, per Amara's framing, common and specifically predictable forecasting mistakes.
stories.sayThis: That's Amara's Law, we overestimate a new technology's short-run impact and underestimate its long-run impact, the same technology, on two different timelines. The internet is the classic example, 1990s predictions about its near-term impact were often overblown, but its actual multi-decade cumulative impact ended up exceeding even that early hype, just on a much longer timeline than anyone originally assumed.
